opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that the money didn't matter. When you're finishing a PhD and companies come to you with offers that are several times what an academic or open-source role pays, that's a real decision. I thought about it seriously.

But what Professor Jordan said stuck with me because he framed it as a question of leverage, not salary. His point was roughly this: a high-paying job means you become one strong engineer inside one company, optimizing that company's systems. vLLM was already becoming infrastructure that many people depended on, including researchers, startups, and big companies. If you keep building that, your work multiplies across the whole ecosystem. That kind of position is rare, and it doesn't come back once you leave it. Money you can always earn later. Being at the center of something at the right moment usually happens once.

He has also watched many waves of technology, from statistics to machine learning to deep learning, and he has a long view of what lasts. He told me open, shared infrastructure tends to outlive any single product cycle. Look at Linux, or the early ML frameworks. The people who built and maintained those ended up shaping the field far more than people who took the obvious lucrative path at the time.

There was a personal part too. I care about the engineering problems in inference: memory management, scheduling, making all kinds of hardware work well. In open source I get the hardest version of those problems, because every model and every accelerator shows up at our door. Inside one company the problem gets narrowed to their stack. So his advice matched something I already felt but hadn't fully admitted to myself: I'd learn more, grow faster, and contribute more by staying.

And it was persuasive because he had no stake in it. He wasn't recruiting me. He was just telling me, as a mentor, what he thought I'd regret or not regret ten years from now. That kind of advice is hard to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response says Jordan had watched multiple technology waves and had a long view of what lasts, grounding his advice in accumulated experience.

r002.rationale: The response says Kaichao chose to stay with vLLM, but does not say he deferred starting a company or believed the timing was not right.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: To be honest, at first I didn't find it persuasive at all. When I finished my PhD, I had offers from big companies, and the numbers were several times what I'd make staying at Berkeley as a postdoc working on vLLM. Any rational calculation says you take the money.

But when I talked to Professor Jordan, he didn't argue about money. He said something like: there are many people who can do a good job at a big company, but there are very few people who are in the position you're in right now. vLLM at that time was growing so fast, every week there was a new model, a new hardware platform, a new problem that nobody had solved yet. He said opportunities like this, where an open-source project becomes the infrastructure the whole field depends on, don't come twice in a career. If you leave, you can always come back to industry. But if you leave now, the project moves on without you, and you can't get this moment back.

The other thing he said that stuck with me is that at this stage, you should optimize for how much you learn and how much impact you have, not how much you earn. Salary compounds slowly. Reputation and the things you understand deeply compound much faster. And in open source, everything you do is public, so if you do good work, people see it. That turned out to be true. A lot of the opportunities I have now came because people saw my work on vLLM, not because of any title.

And frankly, there's a feeling that is hard to explain. When you fix a bug, and the next day thousands of people are running your code to serve their models, that's a kind of satisfaction that a bigger paycheck doesn't give you. So I decided to trust him. Looking back, I think it was the right choice, even though at the time my family wasn't entirely convinced.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Jordan’s advice about vLLM’s rare opportunity and prioritizing learning and impact, but does not say Kaichao found it persuasive because it reflected Jordan’s accumulated experience.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention starting a company or believing the timing was not yet right.

astra-6.text:
What made his advice persuasive was that he was looking beyond the immediate salary difference. With vLLM, I had an opportunity to keep building something that people found useful and help shape where it went. That kind of opportunity is hard to compare directly with a compensation package.

The money mattered, of course. But his advice helped me think about the longer term: where could I learn the most, make a meaningful contribution, and build something I would be proud of? From that perspective, continuing to support vLLM made sense to me.

r001.rationale: The response says Jordan’s advice prompted him to consider long-term learning and contribution, but does not say he found it persuasive because it drew on Jordan’s accumulated experience.

That was the longer-term perspective that made his advice compelling to me.
